control_results.control_name: Network Security Controls: Processes and Mechanisms
control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains general references to security controls review, system documentation updates, and configuration guidance compliance, but lacks specific, formally defined processes and mechanisms for installing and maintaining network security controls as required by PCI DSS. There is no explicit requirement for reviewing network security control configurations at least every 12 months.
evidence: Assesses the performance of security and privacy controls associated with the system/network or web service to ensure the residual risk is maintained within an acceptable range
reviewing at least annually and updating the information system and information system documentation as required into ED's selected central cybersecurity repository (currently CSAM)
Ensures that all IT systems under their purview are configured in accordance with most recent ED and Federal system security configuration guidance
NIST SP 800-41 Revision 1, Guidelines on Firewalls and Firewall Policy, 2009
In coordination with the ISSO, ensures proper physical, administrative, and technical controls are in place
gaps: No formally defined processes and mechanisms specifically for installing and maintaining network security controls (firewalls, network segmentation, IDS/IPS, etc.)
No explicit requirement for reviewing network security control configurations at least every 12 months as specifically required by PCI DSS 1.1
No defined roles or responsibilities specifically for network security control management, rule set reviews, or firewall/router configuration reviews
No documented standards for network security control configuration baselines or change management procedures specific to network security devices
Policy references NIST SP 800-41 (firewall guidance) only as a reference document without operationalizing its requirements
recommendations: Develop a dedicated network security controls policy that formally defines processes for installing, configuring, and maintaining firewalls, routers, and other network security devices
Establish an explicit requirement for reviewing all network security control configurations (firewall rulesets, ACLs, network segmentation policies) at least every 12 months, with documented sign-off
Assign specific roles and responsibilities for network security control ownership, including who is authorized to make changes and who reviews configurations
Create and maintain network security control configuration baselines and implement a formal change management process for any modifications to network security devices
Implement tracking metrics and reporting mechanisms to ensure network security configuration reviews are completed on schedule and findings are remediated

control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains only tangential references to network security concepts such as limiting connections to secure protocols and general access control principles, but does not specifically address configuring network security controls (firewalls, ACLs, etc.) to restrict inbound and outbound traffic with a default-deny posture.
evidence: Limits connections to publicly accessible Federal websites and web services to approved secure protocols.
Limits information system access to authorized users, processes actions on behalf of authorized users, or devices (including other information systems);
Assesses the performance of security and privacy controls associated with the system/network or web service to ensure the residual risk is maintained within an acceptable range
Obtains appropriate interconnection security agreements (ISAs) or memoranda of understanding (MOUs) prior to connecting with other systems and/or sharing sensitive data/information
gaps: No explicit requirement to configure network security controls (firewalls, network segmentation devices) to restrict both inbound and outbound traffic to only necessary communications
No default-deny policy for network traffic is defined
No requirement for documenting and justifying allowed network traffic flows (protocols, ports, services)
No mention of periodic review and maintenance of firewall/network security control rulesets
No specification of rules for denying all traffic not explicitly permitted
No requirement for network diagrams showing traffic flows and security control placement
recommendations: Develop a dedicated network security control configuration policy that mandates a default-deny stance for all inbound and outbound traffic, permitting only explicitly authorized and documented traffic flows
Require documentation of all allowed network traffic rules including business justification, source, destination, ports, and protocols
Establish a periodic review process (at least every six months) for all firewall and network security control rulesets to validate continued business need
Mandate network architecture diagrams that clearly depict cardholder data environment boundaries, traffic flows, and placement of network security controls
Define specific responsibilities for network security control configuration, change management, and ongoing monitoring with defined metrics and accountability

control_results.control_name: Network Access to the Cardholder Data Environment
control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains general references to defense-in-depth, least-privilege access, and limiting connections to approved secure protocols, but it does not specifically address cardholder data environment (CDE) segmentation, DMZ architecture, firewall rules prohibiting direct public access to CDE components, or any PCI DSS-specific network access restrictions.
evidence: The security and privacy controls that provide this protection must meet Federal requirements with additional risk-based and business-driven control implementation achieved through a defense-in-depth security structure.
Access to all ED information must be limited based on a least-privilege approach and a need-to-know basis.
Limits connections to publicly accessible Federal websites and web services to approved secure protocols.
Obtains appropriate interconnection security agreements (ISAs) or memoranda of understanding (MOUs) prior to connecting with other systems and/or sharing sensitive data/information.
gaps: No definition or identification of a cardholder data environment (CDE) or its boundaries
No explicit prohibition of direct public access between the internet and CDE components
No mention of DMZ architecture, network segmentation, or firewall rule sets specific to protecting cardholder data
No requirements for restricting inbound and outbound traffic to only that which is necessary for the CDE
No mention of prohibiting direct routes between the internet and internal CDE systems (e.g., database servers storing cardholder data)
No reference to PCI DSS requirements or payment card data handling controls
recommendations: Define and document the cardholder data environment (CDE) with explicit network boundaries, including identification of all systems that store, process, or transmit cardholder data
Implement and document DMZ architecture requirements that prohibit direct public access to any CDE component, with specific firewall and router rules restricting inbound and outbound traffic
Establish formal network segmentation controls isolating the CDE from untrusted networks and other internal network zones, with documented justification for all allowed traffic flows

Create PCI DSS-specific policies and procedures that address requirements 1.3.1 through 1.3.7, including restricting inbound traffic to only necessary protocols, prohibiting direct internet-to-CDE routes, and implementing anti-spoofing measures
Implement regular reviews and testing of firewall and router configurations to verify that CDE network access restrictions remain effective and properly enforced

control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains general references to configuring systems in accordance with federal security guidance and NIST standards, but there is no specific mention of changing vendor-supplied default passwords, removing or disabling unnecessary default accounts, or defining processes for applying secure configurations to address default credentials.
evidence: Ensures that all IT systems under their purview are configured in accordance with most recent ED and Federal system security configuration guidance, and Federal CIO Council guidance

Ensures the requirements are effectively integrated into IT component products and information systems through purposeful security architecting, design, development, and configuration, following the ED change management processes
Implements proper system backups and patch management processes
gaps: No explicit requirement to change all vendor-supplied default passwords before deploying systems
No process defined for identifying and removing or disabling unnecessary default accounts
No specific mention of secure configuration baselines that address default security parameters (e.g., SNMP community strings, default encryption keys)
No defined process or mechanism specifically for applying and verifying secure configurations related to vendor defaults
No mention of maintaining an inventory of default accounts or credentials that must be addressed prior to deployment
recommendations: Develop and document a formal policy requiring all vendor-supplied default passwords, community strings, and security parameters to be changed before any system is placed into production
Create a process to identify, disable, or remove all unnecessary default accounts on all system components, with documented justification for any retained default accounts
Establish secure configuration baselines (e.g., CIS Benchmarks, STIGs) that explicitly address default credentials and parameters, and mandate their use for all system deployments
Implement automated scanning or verification procedures to detect unchanged default credentials and default accounts across all environments
Integrate default password and account management checks into the existing change management and system authorization processes

control_results.control_name: System Components Configured and Managed Securely
control_results.score_rationale: The policy addresses configuration management at a high level by requiring systems to be configured in accordance with federal and ED security configuration guidance, and assigns responsibilities for maintaining security posture, but lacks specific configuration standards, hardening baselines, or detailed procedures for developing and implementing configuration standards for all system component types.
evidence: Ensures that all IT systems under their purview are configured in accordance with most recent ED and Federal system security configuration guidance, and Federal CIO Council guidance (e.g., OMB M-11-11 and the Federal Identity Credential and Access Management Roadmap and Implementation Guidance)

Follows the guidance found in ED's Common Controls Catalog and the current version of NIST SP 800-53, reviewing at least annually and updating the information system and information system documentation as required

Ensures the requirements are effectively integrated into IT component products and information systems through purposeful security architecting, design, development, and configuration, following the ED change management processes
Implements proper system backups and patch management processes
Ensures that actions are taken to respond and complies within specified timelines for any government-wide or ED-wide directed action items related to vulnerability patching
gaps: No specific configuration standards or hardening baselines defined for different system component types (servers, databases, network devices, endpoints, etc.)
No documented process for developing, maintaining, and approving configuration standards
No requirement to remove or disable unnecessary default accounts, services, protocols, ports, or functions
No mention of industry-accepted hardening standards (e.g., CIS Benchmarks, DISA STIGs) as configuration baselines
No defined process for managing and documenting deviations or exceptions from configuration standards
No requirement for automated configuration monitoring or compliance verification against established baselines
No mention of secure configuration for specific technologies such as wireless, databases, web servers, or applications
recommendations: Develop and document specific configuration standards and hardening baselines for each type of system component, referencing industry benchmarks such as CIS Benchmarks or DISA STIGs
Implement a formal process for creating, reviewing, approving, and updating configuration standards with defined ownership and review cadence
Add explicit requirements to disable unnecessary services, protocols, ports, and default accounts on all system components
Deploy automated configuration compliance monitoring tools to continuously validate system components against approved baselines and report deviations
Establish a formal exception/deviation management process for any departures from approved configuration standards, including risk acceptance documentation
Include specific secure configuration requirements for all technology categories (network devices, servers, databases, applications, containers, cloud services, etc.)

control_results.control_name: Stored Account Data is Kept to Minimum
control_results.score_rationale: The policy excerpts contain no mention of stored account data, cardholder data, payment card data, PCI DSS, or any data retention policies specific to payment card information. The policy focuses entirely on federal cybersecurity compliance (FISMA, NIST, PII/SPII protections) without addressing PCI requirements.
gaps: No definition or documentation of processes for protecting stored account data (e.g., PAN, cardholder data)
No cardholder data retention policy specifying what data is stored, how long it is retained, and when/how it is disposed
No data discovery or inventory process to identify where stored account data resides
No mention of minimizing stored account data or limiting storage to only what is necessary for business purposes
No defined mechanisms for securely deleting cardholder data when it exceeds the defined retention period
No reference to PCI DSS requirements or payment card industry standards
recommendations: Develop and implement a formal cardholder data retention and disposal policy that defines what account data may be stored, where, for how long, and the secure deletion process
Conduct a data discovery exercise to identify all locations where stored account data exists across the environment
Implement automated processes to detect and securely purge cardholder data that exceeds the defined retention period
Document formal processes and mechanisms for protecting stored account data, including encryption, access controls, and masking requirements aligned with PCI DSS 4.0 Requirement 3
Integrate PCI DSS requirements into the existing enterprise cybersecurity policy framework alongside FISMA/NIST controls

control_results.control_name: Access to Cardholder Data is Restricted
control_results.score_rationale: The policy establishes a general principle of least-privilege and need-to-know access to ED information, which partially addresses the access restriction component of the control. However, there is no mention of cardholder data, primary account numbers (PAN), or any requirement to render PAN unreadable anywhere it is stored (e.g., encryption, hashing, truncation, tokenization).
evidence: Access to all ED information must be limited based on a least-privilege approach and a need-to-know basis.
Authorized user access must be limited to only information necessary for the performance of required tasks.

All ED information must be protected from unauthorized access, use, disclosure, duplication, modification, diversion, or destruction—whether accidental or intentional — in order to maintain confidentiality, integrity, and availability.
gaps: No specific mention of cardholder data (CHD) or primary account numbers (PAN) as a data category requiring protection.
No requirement to render PAN unreadable anywhere it is stored (e.g., through encryption, hashing, truncation, or tokenization).
No defined PCI DSS-specific access control procedures for stored account data.
No mention of cryptographic key management for protecting stored cardholder data.
No specific role-based access control (RBAC) framework mapped to cardholder data environments.
No reference to PCI DSS standards or payment card industry requirements anywhere in the policy.
recommendations: Develop a dedicated Cardholder Data Protection policy or appendix that explicitly addresses PCI DSS requirements for restricting access to stored account data based on business need-to-know.

Implement and document technical controls to render PAN unreadable wherever it is stored, using one-way hashes, truncation, index tokens, or strong cryptography with associated key management processes.
Define and maintain a cardholder data inventory identifying all locations where PAN is stored, and enforce role-based access controls specific to those environments.
Integrate PCI DSS compliance requirements into the existing NIST SP 800-53 control framework referenced in the policy, mapping PCI controls to corresponding NIST controls.
Establish monitoring and audit mechanisms to verify that access to cardholder data is appropriately restricted and that PAN rendering controls are functioning as intended.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy document contains no mention of Primary Account Number (PAN), payment card data, or specific requirements for encrypting stored cardholder data. While FIPS 140-2 is referenced in the list of standards, there is no policy language connecting cryptographic requirements to PAN protection.
evidence: FIPS PUB 140-2, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules
gaps: No policy language addressing PAN storage, handling, or protection
No requirement to render PAN unreadable wherever it is stored using strong cryptography (e.g., encryption, truncation, tokenization, or hashing)
No identification of systems or databases that store, process, or transmit cardholder data
No specification of approved cryptographic algorithms or key strengths for PAN encryption
No cryptographic key management procedures specific to PAN protection
No policy defining acceptable PAN display or masking requirements
No data retention and disposal requirements specific to cardholder data
recommendations: Develop a dedicated Cardholder Data Protection policy or addendum that explicitly addresses PAN security requirements per PCI DSS 3.5

Define and document approved methods for rendering PAN unreadable (strong one-way hash functions, truncation, index tokens with securely stored pads, or strong cryptography with associated key management)
Inventory all systems, applications, and storage locations where PAN may be stored and implement encryption controls for each
Establish cryptographic key management procedures aligned with PCI DSS requirements, including key generation, distribution, storage, rotation, and destruction
Implement PAN masking policies so that only personnel with a legitimate business need can view the full PAN
Integrate PAN security requirements into the existing risk assessment and continuous monitoring processes referenced in the policy

control_results.score_rationale: The policy excerpts contain no defined processes or mechanisms specifically addressing the protection of cardholder data with strong cryptography during transmission over open, public networks. The documents reference general NIST frameworks and FIPS 140-2 cryptographic standards in a reference list, but do not define any specific processes, roles, or requirements related to PCI cardholder data transmission protection.
evidence: FIPS PUB 140-2, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules
NIST Special Publications 800-52, Guidelines for the Selection and Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) Implementations, 2014
OMB M-15-13, Policy to Require Secure Connections across Federal Websites and Web Services, 2015
gaps: No definition or mention of cardholder data (CHD) or payment card data protection requirements
No documented processes or mechanisms for protecting data with strong cryptography during transmission over open, public networks
No specification of approved cryptographic protocols (e.g., TLS 1.2+) or cipher suites for data in transit
No roles and responsibilities defined for managing cryptographic protections of cardholder data
No documentation that these processes are understood by relevant personnel as required by PCI-DSS 4.1
No inventory or identification of trusted keys and certificates used for transmission protection
No policy statements prohibiting the use of insecure protocols (e.g., SSL, early TLS) for cardholder data transmission
recommendations: Develop a dedicated policy or policy section that explicitly addresses protection of cardholder data during transmission over open, public networks with strong cryptography, specifying approved protocols (TLS 1.2 or higher) and prohibited protocols
Define and document roles, responsibilities, and accountability for personnel involved in managing cryptographic controls for cardholder data transmission
Establish procedures to maintain an inventory of trusted keys and certificates, including lifecycle management (generation, distribution, storage, rotation, and revocation)
Implement a training and awareness program to ensure all relevant personnel understand the processes and mechanisms for protecting cardholder data during transmission
Integrate PCI-DSS requirements into the existing NIST-based security control framework, mapping PCI-4.1 requirements to corresponding NIST SP 800-53 controls (e.g., SC-8, SC-13)

control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains only tangential references to secure protocols and cryptographic standards (e.g., limiting connections to 'approved secure protocols,' referencing FIPS 140-2 and NIST SP 800-52 for TLS), but does not specifically address PAN protection during transmission, strong cryptography requirements for cardholder data, trusted key/certificate management, or secure protocol version enforcement.
evidence: Limits connections to publicly accessible Federal websites and web services to approved secure protocols.
FIPS PUB 140-2, Security Requirements for Cryptographic Modules
NIST SP 800-52 Revision 1, Guidelines for the Selection, Configuration, and Use of Transport Layer Security (TLS) Implementations, 2014
gaps: No explicit requirement to protect PANs (Primary Account Numbers) with strong cryptography during transmission
No policy language specifying that only trusted keys and certificates are accepted for transmission security
No requirement to ensure protocols in use only support secure versions and configurations (e.g., TLS 1.2 or higher mandated)
No mention of PCI DSS scope, cardholder data environments, or PAN-specific data handling procedures
No defined process for certificate management, validation, or revocation during data transmission

recommendations: Develop a specific PCI DSS-aligned policy section that mandates strong cryptography (e.g., TLS 1.2+) for all transmission of PANs and cardholder data
Establish a trusted key and certificate management policy that includes procedures for validating certificates, managing certificate authorities, and rejecting untrusted or expired certificates
Define and enforce approved secure protocol versions and configurations, explicitly prohibiting deprecated protocols such as SSL, TLS 1.0, and TLS 1.1
Implement monitoring and logging mechanisms to detect and alert on any PAN transmissions using non-compliant encryption methods
Integrate PCI DSS requirements into the existing cybersecurity policy framework with clear roles and responsibilities for protecting cardholder data in transit

control_results.score_rationale: The policy excerpts contain no mention of anti-malware solutions, malware protection processes, or mechanisms for deploying and managing anti-malware across systems. The documents focus on general cybersecurity governance roles, responsibilities, access control, and references to NIST frameworks but do not address malware protection specifically.
gaps: No defined processes or mechanisms for protecting systems against malware
No requirement for deploying anti-malware solutions on all system components

No mention of malware detection, prevention, or remediation capabilities
No policy language addressing anti-malware solution configuration, updates, or monitoring

control_results.score_rationale: The policy excerpts contain no specific mention of anti-malware mechanisms, solutions, scanning, or malware protection processes. gaps: No policy language requiring deployment of anti-malware solutions on systems
No requirements for regular anti-malware signature/definition updates

Establish requirements for automatic and regular updates of anti-malware signatures and engines with defined frequency

control_results.control_name: Bespoke and Custom Software Developed Securely
control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains general references to secure development practices such as integrating security requirements into system design, development, and configuration, but there is no explicit mention of secure coding guidelines, OWASP Top 10, code review processes, or specific secure software development lifecycle (SDLC) practices required by PCI-6.2.
evidence: Ensures the requirements are effectively integrated into IT component products and information systems through purposeful security architecting, design, development, and configuration, following the ED change management processes

Identifies, tailors, documents, and implements information security and privacy-related functional requirements necessary to protect ED information, information systems, missions, and business processes
gaps: No reference to secure coding guidelines or standards such as OWASP Top 10
No requirement for code reviews (manual or automated) during the development process
No mention of software development lifecycle (SDLC) security practices specific to bespoke and custom software
No requirement for vulnerability testing (e.g., static analysis, dynamic analysis, penetration testing) of custom-developed software
No training requirements for developers on secure coding practices
No mention of input validation, output encoding, authentication controls, or other specific secure coding techniques
No defined process for addressing and remediating coding vulnerabilities before deployment
recommendations: Develop and document a formal Secure Software Development Lifecycle (SSDLC) policy that explicitly addresses PCI DSS 6.2 requirements for bespoke and custom software
Mandate adherence to OWASP Top 10 and other recognized secure coding standards (e.g., CERT, SANS) for all custom development
Require mandatory secure coding training for all developers, with periodic refreshers
Implement mandatory code review processes (both manual peer reviews and automated static/dynamic analysis) before code is promoted to production
Define specific controls for common vulnerability categories including injection flaws, broken authentication, XSS, insecure deserialization, and other OWASP Top 10 categories
Establish metrics and accountability mechanisms to track secure development compliance and remediation of identified coding vulnerabilities

control_results.score_rationale: The policy assigns responsibility for vulnerability patching and compliance with directed timelines, and requires capturing weaknesses in POA&Ms, but it lacks a formally defined vulnerability management process, does not specify a 30-day critical patch installation requirement, and does not detail vulnerability identification procedures such as scanning cadence or severity classification.
evidence: Ensures that security patches for all assigned information systems are installed within the timeframe identified by ED policy;
In support of the ISO, ensures that actions are taken to respond and comply within specified timelines for any government-wide or ED-wide directed action items related to vulnerability patching;
This includes actions directed by the DHS, which issues "Binding Operational Directives" (BODs), that mandate reporting requirements by the Department for remediating critical vulnerabilities;
Ensures that information security notices and advisories are distributed to appropriate ED and contractor personnel and that vendor-issued security patches are expeditiously installed;
Ensures that system weaknesses are captured in the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) and are entered into ED's selected Central Cybersecurity Repository (currently CSAM);
gaps: No explicit requirement to install critical patches within 30 days as required by PCI-6.3; the policy only references 'the timeframe identified by ED policy' without specifying that timeframe.
No formally documented vulnerability management process or lifecycle (identification, classification, prioritization, remediation, verification).
No defined vulnerability scanning cadence or methodology (e.g., periodic automated scanning, penetration testing schedules).
No severity classification scheme or risk-ranking criteria for identified vulnerabilities.
No defined metrics or KPIs for tracking vulnerability remediation performance and compliance.
No process for evaluating and addressing vulnerabilities in custom or third-party software prior to deployment.
recommendations: Define and document a comprehensive vulnerability management process covering identification (scanning frequency, tools), classification (severity ratings), prioritization, remediation timelines, and verification.
Explicitly mandate that critical and high-severity patches be installed within 30 days of release, aligning with PCI-6.3 requirements, and document this timeframe in the policy.
Establish regular vulnerability scanning requirements (e.g., monthly or quarterly automated scans, annual penetration testing) with defined scope and reporting.
Implement a vulnerability severity classification scheme (e.g., CVSS-based) with corresponding remediation SLAs for each severity level.
Define metrics and reporting mechanisms (e.g., mean time to remediate, percentage of systems patched within SLA) with accountability to senior management.
Incorporate secure development and vulnerability assessment requirements for custom and third-party applications before deployment into production.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy formally documents multiple access control mechanisms including least privilege, separation of duties, need-to-know access determination, quarterly account reviews, and defined roles/responsibilities for privileged users. However, it lacks explicit reference to cardholder data environments, PCI-specific scoping, and formal documentation of access control processes as a standalone defined procedure with metrics and monitoring.
evidence: Limits information system access to authorized users, processes actions on behalf of authorized users, or devices (including other information systems);
Limits information system access to the types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute;
Employs the principle of least privilege, including for specific security functions and privileged accounts;

Determines who should be granted access to the system and with what rights and privileges, and grants users the fewest possible privileges necessary for job performance in order to ensure privileges are based on a legitimate need;
Conducts quarterly reviews and validations of system users' accounts to ensure the continued need for access to a system;
Enforces the concept of separation of duties by ensuring that no single individual has control of the entirety of any critical process in coordination with the ISSO;
Shares only the minimum PII from ED systems and applications that is necessary and relevant for the purposes it was originally collected.
gaps: No explicit reference to cardholder data (CHD) or cardholder data environments (CDE) — access control processes are not scoped to PCI DSS requirements specifically.
No formally documented access control policy that is explicitly defined and communicated as required by PCI-7.1 (i.e., ensuring processes are 'defined and understood' by all relevant personnel).
No evidence of a formal process for defining business need-to-know specifically tied to system components storing, processing, or transmitting cardholder data.
No mention of periodic review or update cadence for the access control policy/processes themselves to ensure they remain current and understood.
No evidence of metrics, KPIs, or monitoring mechanisms to measure the effectiveness of access control processes.
recommendations: Develop a PCI-specific access control policy that explicitly addresses restricting access to system components and cardholder data by business need to know, referencing CDE scope.
Formally document and communicate access control processes to all relevant personnel, ensuring they are 'defined and understood' with evidence of acknowledgment (e.g., sign-off or training records).
Establish a formal role-based access control (RBAC) matrix mapping job functions to specific access levels for cardholder data and CDE system components.
Implement a defined review cycle (at least annually) for the access control policy and processes to ensure they remain current and effective.
Introduce measurable metrics (e.g., percentage of accounts reviewed on schedule, number of access violations detected) to move toward a managed maturity level.

control_results.control_name: Access to System Components and Data
control_results.score_rationale: The policy formally defines and documents least-privilege access principles, role-based access assignment, quarterly access reviews, separation of duties, and restrictions on privileged accounts, covering all major elements of the control with measurable accountability mechanisms.
evidence: Access to all ED information must be limited based on a least-privilege approach and a need-to-know basis.
Authorized user access must be limited to only information necessary for the performance of required tasks.

Determines who should be granted access to the system and with what rights and privileges, and grants users the fewest possible privileges necessary for job performance in order to ensure privileges are based on a legitimate need;
Conducts quarterly reviews and validations of system users' accounts to ensure the continued need for access to a system;
Enforces the concept of separation of duties by ensuring that no single individual has control of the entirety of any critical process in coordination with the ISSO;
Employs the principle of least privilege, including for specific security functions and privileged accounts;
Limits information system access to authorized users, processes actions on behalf of authorized users, or devices (including other information systems);
Limits information system access to the types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute;

utilize PIV based authentication approaches

based authenticators, and personal identification numbers (PIN) and passwords that are compliant with FIPS publications;
OMB M-11-11, Continued Implementation of Homeland Security Presidential Directive (HSPD) 12– Policy for a Common Identification Standard for Federal Employees and Contractors
gaps: No explicit requirement for MFA for all non-console administrative access to the cardholder data environment (CDE)
No explicit requirement for MFA for all remote network access
No definition of what constitutes acceptable MFA factors (something you know, something you have, something you are) in the context of CDE access
No mention of cardholder data environment or PCI DSS scope
No specific procedures for enforcing MFA at network or system entry points to the CDE
No monitoring or metrics defined for MFA compliance or enforcement
recommendations: Develop and document an explicit MFA policy that requires multi-factor authentication for all non-console administrative access to the cardholder data environment
Mandate MFA for all remote network access originating from outside the trusted network, specifying at least two of the three authentication factor categories
Identify and document all access points into the CDE and map MFA enforcement mechanisms to each
Establish monitoring and reporting processes to verify MFA is consistently enforced and to detect any bypass attempts
Integrate PCI DSS 8.4 MFA requirements with the existing PIV/HSPD-12 program to leverage existing infrastructure while ensuring CDE-specific coverage

control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains only tangential references to auditing (e.g., 'audit the execution of such function' for privileged functions) but does not establish a formal audit logging program, does not specify what events must be logged, and makes no mention of cardholder data access logging or forensic analysis capabilities.
evidence: Prevents non-privileged users from executing privileged functions and audit the execution of such function.
Limits information system access to authorized users, processes actions on behalf of authorized users, or devices (including other information systems)
Limits information system access to the types of transactions and functions that authorized users are permitted to execute
gaps: No requirement to log all individual user access to cardholder data

No definition of specific audit log events to be captured (e.g., user access, authentication attempts, changes to accounts, access to audit logs, invalid access attempts, use of identification and authentication mechanisms)
No requirement for audit logs to support detection of anomalies and suspicious activity
No requirement for forensic analysis capabilities or log retention policies
No mention of automated audit log monitoring, alerting, or review processes
No reference to cardholder data environment (CDE) or PCI DSS logging requirements
No specification of log content requirements (e.g., user identification, event type, date/time, success/failure, origination, identity of affected data/resource)
recommendations: Develop and implement a comprehensive audit logging policy that specifies all events to be captured per PCI DSS 10.2 sub-requirements, including individual access to cardholder data, administrative actions, access to audit trails, invalid logical access attempts, and use of authentication mechanisms

Define audit log content requirements ensuring each log entry includes user identification, event type, date and time, success or failure indication, origination of event, and identity of affected data, system component, or resource
Implement centralized log management with automated monitoring and alerting to support anomaly and suspicious activity detection
Establish log retention and protection policies to ensure logs are available for forensic analysis
Integrate audit logging requirements into the existing access control framework and assign clear accountability for log review and monitoring

control_results.score_rationale: The policy excerpts contain no mention of time synchronization technology, NTP/PTP protocols, authoritative time sources, consistent time settings across systems, or protection of time data from unauthorized modification. None of the requirements of PCI 10.6 are addressed.
gaps: No policy or procedure for deploying time synchronization technology (e.g., NTP, PTP)
No requirement for systems to receive time from designated, authoritative internal or external time sources
No guidance on ensuring consistent and correct time across all systems
No controls specified for protecting time data from unauthorized modification
No restrictions on which personnel can modify time settings or time-related configurations
No monitoring or alerting mechanisms for time synchronization drift or failures
recommendations: Develop and document a formal time synchronization policy specifying the use of NTP or equivalent technology with designated authoritative time sources (e.g., NIST Internet Time Service, GPS-based sources)
Require all critical systems, network devices, and servers to synchronize to approved internal time servers and define acceptable drift thresholds
Implement access controls restricting the ability to modify time settings to authorized personnel only, and log all changes to time configurations
Establish monitoring and alerting for time synchronization failures or significant drift across the environment
Include time synchronization configuration requirements in system hardening and configuration management baselines
Periodically review and validate that time synchronization is functioning correctly across all in-scope systems as part of ongoing compliance checks

control_results.score_rationale: The policy references continuous monitoring, incident response reporting, and FISMA metrics reporting at a general level, but does not specifically address detection, alerting, and prompt response to failures of critical security controls, nor does it mention the use of log management tools to facilitate log reviews.
evidence: Ensures continuous monitoring of the information system's security is performed and validates the information system against the System Security Plan (SSP) while managing and controlling any information system updates
Reports and responds to cybersecurity incidents in accordance with ED's Information Security Incident Response and Reporting Procedures
Assesses the performance of security and privacy controls associated with the system/network or web service to ensure the residual risk is maintained within an acceptable range

Ensures that a PO-level asset, data, and information security continuous monitoring strategy is developed and implemented to enable ongoing visibility into the cybersecurity risk posture of each information system within the PO
gaps: No specific requirement to detect failures of critical security controls (e.g., firewall failures, IDS/IPS failures, antivirus failures, access control mechanism failures)
No defined process for alerting and reporting when critical security controls fail
No mention of log management tools or automated mechanisms to facilitate log reviews
No defined response timelines or escalation procedures specifically for security control failures
No mention of monitoring mechanisms for logging system failures or anomalies in audit log generation
recommendations: Develop and document a formal process for detecting, alerting, and responding to failures of critical security controls, including specific controls to monitor (firewalls, IDS/IPS, antivirus, access controls, audit logging mechanisms)
Implement and document the use of log management tools (e.g., SIEM) to aggregate, correlate, and facilitate review of security logs across all critical systems
Define specific response timelines and escalation procedures for when critical security control failures are detected
Establish automated alerting mechanisms that notify security personnel promptly when critical security controls cease functioning
Include periodic testing of failure detection and response capabilities to ensure they function as intended

control_results.score_rationale: The policy establishes a comprehensive enterprise-wide Information Security Program (ISP) with defined roles, responsibilities, and a structured policy framework. However, there is no explicit requirement for the information security policy itself to be reviewed at least once every 12 months; the annual review mention pertains to information system documentation rather than the overarching security policy.
evidence: ED must implement an Enterprise-wide ISP that provides policies, instructions, standards, and guidance to ensure the protection of its information and information systems.
ED must develop and maintain the information security policies and associated cybersecurity instructions for the ISP.
reviews information system documentation and the information system itself at least annually

The structure of this policy framework is illustrated in Figure 1 below. It illustrates a framework that fully supports the strategic, operational, and tactical level needs of the ED for all cybersecurity policy

Information security is an enterprise-wide and individual responsibility that is shared by Senior Agency Officials, all ED managers and staff, Business/ Information/System Owners, IT professionals, and all other users of ED information and information systems.
gaps: No explicit requirement that the information security policy itself is reviewed at least once every 12 months and updated as needed — the annual review referenced applies to information system documentation, not the overarching ISP.
No defined process or responsible party specifically assigned to conduct the annual policy review cycle.
No evidence of a mechanism to ensure the policy is 'known' to all relevant personnel (e.g., distribution, acknowledgment, or awareness requirements specifically tied to the ISP).
No defined metrics or tracking to confirm the policy remains current and that reviews are completed on schedule.
recommendations: Add an explicit requirement that the comprehensive information security policy is formally reviewed at least annually and updated as needed, with a defined owner responsible for the review.
Establish a documented process for annual policy review that includes version control, review dates, approval signatures, and change tracking.
Implement a mechanism (e.g., mandatory acknowledgment, training, or distribution log) to ensure the policy is known and communicated to all relevant stakeholders.
Define metrics and reporting to track policy review completion dates and ensure accountability for keeping the policy current.

control_results.score_rationale: The policy contains several risk-related activities including residual risk identification, risk assessments for unauthorized access/disclosure, and POA&M tracking, but it lacks a formal, documented risk assessment process specifically targeting the cardholder data environment and does not meet the PCI requirement for at least annual risk assessments (the policy specifies every three years or upon significant changes).
evidence: Identifies residual risk and provides justification for AO risk decisions

Conducts assessments of the risk and magnitude of the harm that would result from the unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, or destruction of information and information systems that support the Department's critical operations, at no less than every three years or when significant changes occur to the system/network
Ensures that system weaknesses are captured in the Plan of Action and Milestones (POA&M) and are entered into ED's selected Central Cybersecurity Repository (currently CSAM)

Ensures that privacy is addressed throughout the life cycle of ED's information system, and that Federal privacy requirements are incorporated into the agency's enterprise architecture to ensure that risk is addressed and information systems achieve the necessary levels of trustworthiness, protection, and resilience
gaps: No formal risk assessment process specifically targeting the cardholder data environment (CDE) as required by PCI DSS
Risk assessments are required only every three years, not at least annually as PCI 12.3 mandates
No documented methodology for identifying, evaluating, and managing risks specific to payment card data
No mention of cardholder data, payment card data, or PCI DSS scope in the risk assessment process
No defined process for maintaining a risk register or tracking risk treatment decisions specific to CDE assets
No evidence of formal risk evaluation criteria or risk acceptance thresholds for cardholder data risks
recommendations: Develop and document a formal risk assessment methodology specifically for the cardholder data environment that aligns with PCI DSS 12.3 requirements
Increase the frequency of risk assessments to at least annually for systems processing, storing, or transmitting cardholder data
Create and maintain a CDE-specific risk register that documents identified risks, evaluation results, risk treatment decisions, and residual risk acceptance
Define formal risk evaluation criteria, impact/likelihood scales, and risk acceptance thresholds tailored to cardholder data risks
Integrate PCI-specific risk assessment outputs into the existing POA&M process and CSAM repository to ensure tracking and accountability
Assign explicit roles and responsibilities for conducting and reviewing PCI-scoped risk assessments on an annual basis
